source.title: Landscaper: Understanding Loss Landscapes Through Multi-Dimensional Topological Analysis
source.authors: Jia-Qing Chen; N. Hadler; Tiankai Xie; Rostyslav Hnatyshyn; Caleb Geniesse; Yaoqing Yang; Michael W. Mahoney; T. Perciano; John F. Hartwig; Ross Maciejewski; Gunther H. Weber

record.file_problem: Supplied full paper text; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: Measures loss-landscape properties alongside train/test or OOD performance using SMAD and Hessian trace, a different method from the listed claim versions. Its direct results concern landscape geometry and OOD prediction rather than the specified standard-training generalization comparisons.
record.gate_note: Rows record the paper's own outcomes relating landscape measurements to train/test or OOD performance. It does not test memorization of random labels, width beyond interpolation, CNN-versus-fully-connected generalization, optimizer or batch-size comparisons, dropout effects, magnitude-aware sharpness, or removal of memorized examples. Cited prior work is not recorded as a result.
record.test_reason: The study reports landscape geometry and its associations with predictive performance, but tests none of V1–V8. SMAD and Hessian trace do not measure V7's magnitude-scaled perturbation tolerance or its ranking of generalization gaps. The CIFAR-10 regimes jointly change training size, duration, regularization and augmentation, providing no isolated test of V5 or V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes the authors' conclusion: SMAD captures global topological structure complementary to local curvature and is a promising OOD-performance proxy in the catalyst task, requiring broader validation. Its demonstrated OOD prediction uses landscapes evaluated on ID test data, and the six-configuration sample warrants caution.
record.recipe_differences: The paper measures loss-landscape metrics and their associations with performance, rather than testing the interventions or comparisons in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Landscape metric associations differ by architecture/task: Hessian trace correlated with performance gaps for the two QM9 model families, while SMAD did not; SMAD correlated with OOD RMSE in the catalyst task. For MultiBERTs Seed 2, SMAD and Hessian trace move in opposite directions from 20k to 40k steps.

fits_no_version.finding: Across CIFAR-10 regimes, the well-fit CNN has the lowest SMAD (0.130) and highest test accuracy (0.879); the overfit CNN has the highest SMAD (0.294). The underfit CNN has the smallest train–test accuracy gap (0.059), despite intermediate SMAD.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SMAD distinguishes these bundled training regimes and coincides with their qualitative geometry; this comparison does not establish a monotonic relationship with generalization gaps.

fits_no_version.finding: Across ten QM9 targets, inter-model Hessian-trace differences correlate with performance differences (ρ = −0.77, p = 0.009); SMAD has no significant association.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In the tested SchNet–DimeNet++ comparison, Hessian trace tracks predictive-performance differences more clearly than SMAD.

fits_no_version.finding: From 20k to 40k steps for MultiBERTs Seed 2, SMAD falls from 0.107 to 0.065 while Hessian trace rises from 533.63 to 5412.79.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Topological simplification can accompany increased local curvature during this training transition.

fits_no_version.finding: Across six catalyst-model configurations, ID-test-landscape SMAD correlates with OOD RMSE (ρ = 0.928); adding log10(SMAD) reduces OOD-prediction LOOCV RMSE from 0.135 to 0.020.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SMAD contributes predictive information about OOD error beyond ID error in this small configuration set.

record.problems: The authors caution that the catalyst-task sample size is small. The paper states further validation is needed across additional domains, architectures, data regimes, and large-scale training environments. The CIFAR regime comparison changes several training conditions together, so it does not isolate their individual effects.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, chance-level random-label held-out accuracy, and comparison with natural-label generalization under the same recipe.
Test error as width increases beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image-classification performance and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under specified tuning budgets.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adapted training recipes.
Dropout's effect on held-out error, isolated from other training changes.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, its association with generalization gaps among similarly fitted networks, and ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: No version-specific verdict is warranted. The omitted skip-connection and higher-dimensional connectivity results also fit no listed version, so they are not missing version-bearing results.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width sweep beyond interpolation and test-error behavior.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization comparisons.
Adaptive optimizer versus SGD generalization comparisons.
Magnitude-aware sharpness measured against generalization gaps.
Effect of removing memorized examples on test accuracy.

rows.subject: CNN
rows.stage_stated: trained for 5 epochs on a 5,000-sample subset
rows.operation_detail: Trained in the underfit regime; reported train accuracy, test accuracy, and SMAD.
rows.note: Authors describe SMAD as intermediate relative to well-fit and overfit regimes; this row does not test one of V1–V8.
rows.check: Values and conditions match Table 3, but neither SMAD nor this bundled training regime establishes an effect named by a version.

rows.subject: CNN
rows.stage_stated: trained for up to 80 epochs on the full training set
rows.operation_detail: Trained in the well-fit regime; reported train accuracy, test accuracy, and SMAD.
rows.note: Lowest SMAD among the three regimes; paper describes this as the best-generalizing, smoother regime.
rows.check: Values and conditions match Table 3. Comparison with the other regimes cannot isolate dropout or batch-size effects, and SMAD is not V7's measure.

rows.subject: CNN
rows.operation_detail: Trained in the overfit regime; reported train accuracy, test accuracy, and SMAD.
rows.note: Highest SMAD and lower test accuracy than the well-fit regime; authors describe increased global roughness.
rows.check: Values and conditions match Table 3. Perfect natural-label training accuracy does not establish V1's random-label memorization comparison.

rows.subject: SchNet and DimeNet++
rows.operation_detail: Compared Hessian trace and MAE across QM9 regression targets; reported correlation between inter-model trace differences and performance gaps.
rows.measure: Spearman correlation between inter-model Hessian trace differences and performance gaps
rows.note: The paper says SMAD was not significantly correlated with inter-model performance differences; no single correlation number is supplied for that result.
rows.check: The reported correlation matches the text, but compares Hessian-trace differences with predictive-performance differences across two architectures, rather than magnitude-aware sharpness with train–test gaps.

rows.subject: MultiBERTs (Seed 2)
rows.operation_detail: Measured Hessian eigenvalue, Hessian trace, and SMAD across a training transition.
rows.note: Paper characterizes the transition as sharper by spectral metrics but smoother by SMAD; it does not provide train/test error for these checkpoints.
rows.check: Checkpoint values match Table 5, but no generalization outcome is measured for this transition.

rows.subject: 3D GNNs trained with varying augmentation and feature engineering
rows.operation_detail: Compared ID landscape SMAD with ID and OOD test performance across augmentation and feature-engineering configurations.
rows.measure: Correlation of ID-landscape SMAD with OOD RMSE; LOOCV RMSE predicting OOD RMSE from ID RMSE with and without log10(SMAD)
rows.baseline: LOOCV RMSE 0.135 for baseline using ID RMSE
rows.value: Spearman’s ρ = 0.928, p = 0.008; adding log10(SMAD) reduced LOOCV RMSE 0.135 → 0.020 (∆ = 0.115)
rows.note: Authors state the 10-fold augmented model had the lowest OOD RMSE and lowest SMAD. They caution that the sample size is small.
rows.check: The correlations and LOOCV values match the text. Landscapes use the literature ID test dataset, not solely training data. Table 6 rounds both 10-Fold and Charge OOD RMSE to 0.50, so a uniquely best OOD RMSE is not established by the displayed values. The LOOCV result evaluates the proposed predictor rather than any claim version.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
